endorsements.quote: Clinicians also need continual, required training in the specific strengths and failure modes of the AI tools they use in practice.
Professional development should focus on building the skills that are most at risk from AI use [ 10 , 32 , 42 ].

And harm reporting asks whether standardised AI incident-reporting infrastructure is being built in primary care, equivalent to the systems that already exist for medication errors and adverse events.
Technical performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, and recall are necessary but not enough.

unlisted_practices: Protect time for clinical reflection and relationship-based care so that AI efficiency gains do not shorten visits or weaken clinician-patient relationships.
Strengthen rather than cut foundational medical training in clinical reasoning, human biology, and the limits of the evidence base underlying AI systems.
Evaluate AI in primary care on continuity of care, deskilling, patient experience, and patient trust in addition to technical accuracy.
Monitor clinicians for atrophy of reflective clinical reasoning caused by AI use.
Treat AI outputs as provisional artifacts requiring clinical interpretation rather than autonomous judgments.
Establish clear legal, ethical, and regulatory accountability frameworks for clinical decisions shaped by AI outputs.
Involve GPs in AI evaluation, safety protocols, and governance, including feedback and annotation of AI performance in everyday practice.

screen.reason: Editorial providing recommendations and perspectives on how generative AI should be governed, evaluated, and aligned with relational primary care practice.
